case.case_title: Wickramasinghe v. Edmund Jayasinghe, Secretary, Ministry of Media, Tourism and Aviation
case.source_citation: [1995] 1 Sri LR. Supreme Court, decided on 7 November 1995

clause.text: Freedom of speech and expression including publication.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the Emergency (Restriction of Publication and Transmission of Sensitive Military Information) Regulations No. 1 of 1995, which imposed pre-censorship on publication of military-related news, violated the petitioner's fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the regulations imposed a blanket censorship that stifled legitimate criticism of government military policy, were ultra vires, and violated his fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a). He also claimed discrimination as state-controlled and foreign media were allowed self-regulation while he was subjected to strict censorship.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondent argued that the regulations were validly made under the wide powers granted by Section 5 of the Public Security Ordinance in the interest of national security during an ongoing civil war. The restrictions were necessary and not a blanket censorship, and the Competent Authority retained discretionary power to enforce the regulations fairly. The situation justified the restrictions on publication of sensitive military information.
key_facts: The petitioner is Chief Editor and Publisher of the weekly Sinhala newspaper 'Janajaya'.
Emergency regulations prohibited publication of news related to military operations, procurement, deployment, and official conduct of armed forces.
Petitioner ceased publication of military-related news due to regulations but was not prosecuted or stopped from publishing the newspaper.
Some other newspapers, including state-controlled and foreign media, were allowed self-regulation censorship.
The country was in a state of national crisis and ongoing civil war at the time of the regulations.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court recognized that Article 14(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression including publication, but this right is subject to restrictions prescribed by law in the interest of national security and public order. The Court held that the power to impose emergency regulations under the Public Security Ordinance is very wide and the regulations must be considered in the context of the ongoing civil war and national crisis. The Court found that the regulations were not a blanket censorship but targeted sensitive military information, and the Competent Authority's discretionary power to enforce the regulations provided safeguards against arbitrary censorship.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court noted that the petitioner voluntarily ceased publication of military-related news and was not prevented from publishing his newspaper or prosecuted. The Court found no prima facie case that the regulations were ultra vires or violated the petitioner's fundamental rights. The Court also rejected the claim of discrimination, holding that allowing some media self-regulation did not amount to abdication of power or unlawful discrimination.
principles_established: Freedom of speech under Article 14(1)(a) can be restricted by law in the interest of national security and public order.
Emergency regulations made under wide discretionary powers of the President are presumptively valid unless shown to be ultra vires or arbitrary.
Pre-censorship is not necessarily unconstitutional if it is guided by objective standards and justified by national security concerns.
Discretionary enforcement by a Competent Authority can provide a safeguard against absolute censorship.
Claims of discrimination require proof of abdication of power or arbitrary treatment, not mere differences in regulatory approach.
precedents_cited: Hettiarachchi v. Seneviratne et al S.C. App 127/94
Joseph Perera v. The Attorney General [1992] 1 Sri L.R. 199
New York Times v. US [1971] 403 US 713
Organisation for a Better Austin v. Kiefe (1971) 402 US 415

outcome.holding: The Court refused leave to proceed, holding that the petitioner had not made out a prima facie case that the emergency regulations violated his fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a). The regulations were validly imposed in the interest of national security during an ongoing civil war.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression including publication, which the petitioner claimed was infringed by the emergency regulations imposing pre-censorship on military-related news. The Court's reasoning and ultimate dismissal of the petition directly hinged on the interpretation and application of this constitutional right in the context of national security.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner claimed the regulations imposed a blanket censorship violating Article 14(1)(a). The Court held the regulations were justified restrictions in the interest of national security during an ongoing civil war and not a blanket censorship. The petitioner was not prevented from publishing but voluntarily ceased military-related news. Leave to proceed was refused.
